tf.statement: Every local minimizer of a convex function over a convex feasible set is a global minimizer.
tf.explanation: If a feasible point had a lower objective, points on the segment toward it would be feasible, arbitrarily close to the local minimizer, and have a lower objective by convexity.

tf.statement: A differentiable function is convex whenever its gradient vanishes at at least one point.
tf.explanation: For \(f(x)=-x^2\), the gradient vanishes at zero, which is a global maximum. Convexity requires the global convexity inequality; for twice continuously differentiable functions on an open convex domain, it is equivalent to a positive semidefinite Hessian throughout that domain.

tf.statement: The feasible set defined by convex inequalities \(f_i(x)\le0\) and affine equalities is convex.
tf.explanation: Each convex sublevel set is convex, affine equality sets are convex, and intersections preserve convexity.

tf.statement: The Lagrange dual function is concave even when the primal objective or inequality constraints are nonconvex.
tf.explanation: For a fixed primal variable, the Lagrangian is affine in the multipliers. Taking its pointwise infimum produces a concave function, possibly with value \(-\infty\).

tf.statement: For a minimization problem with constraints \(f_i(x)\le0\), every real multiplier vector provides a valid dual lower bound.
tf.explanation: The lower-bound proof uses \(\lambda_i\ge0\), ensuring \(\lambda_if_i(x)\le0\) at a feasible point. Negative inequality multipliers generally break that step.

tf.statement: Equality multipliers may have either sign because the corresponding constraint values are zero at every primal feasible point.
tf.explanation: If \(h_j(x)=0\), then \(\nu_jh_j(x)=0\) for every real \(\nu_j\). Inequality multipliers have a different sign restriction.

tf.statement: If a constraint is active at a KKT point, its multiplier must be strictly positive.
tf.explanation: Complementary slackness only states \(\lambda_if_i(x)=0\). For minimizing \(x^2\) subject to \(-x\le0\), \(x=0\) is active and the KKT multiplier is zero.

tf.statement: At a KKT point, a strictly positive inequality multiplier implies that the corresponding inequality is active.
Every differentiable convex problem with an attained optimum has an optimal finite multiplier vector.
tf.explanation: Consider minimizing \(x\) subject to \(x^2\le0\). The sole feasible point and optimum is zero, but stationarity would require \(1+2\lambda\cdot0=0\), which no finite multiplier satisfies. Regularity conditions matter when asserting multiplier existence or dual attainment.

tf.statement: For a symmetric matrix \(Q\), the unconstrained quadratic \(f(x)=\frac12x^TQx+c^Tx\) is convex if and only if \(Q\succeq0\).
tf.explanation: The Hessian is the constant matrix \(Q\); apply the second-order convexity criterion on \(\mathbb R^n\).

tf.statement: For differentiable convex objectives, every positive constant gradient-descent step size guarantees convergence from every starting point.
tf.explanation: For \(f(x)=x^2/2\), the update is \(x_{k+1}=(1-\eta)x_k\). Taking \(\eta=3\) makes nonzero iterates grow in magnitude. A step-size restriction is needed.

tf.statement: If a primal feasible point and a dual feasible point have the same finite objective value, they certify primal and dual optimality.
tf.explanation: Weak duality gives \(g(\lambda,\nu)\le d^*\le p^*\le f_0(x)\). Equality of the endpoints makes every inequality an equality.

mc.stem: Which formulations satisfy the definition of a convex optimization problem? All variables shown are real.

options.text: Minimize \(x^2+y^2\) subject to \(x+y=1\) and \(x\ge0\).
options.why: The objective is convex, the equality is affine, and the inequality defines a half-space.

options.text: Minimize \(-x^2\) subject to \(-1\le x\le1\).
options.why: The feasible set is convex, but the minimization objective is concave and not convex.

options.text: Minimize \(x\) subject to \(x^2=1\).
options.why: The equality produces the nonconvex feasible set \(\{-1,1\}\); nonlinear equalities cannot generally be treated as affine constraints.

options.text: Minimize \(3x-y\) subject to \(x^2+y^2\le4\).
options.why: The objective is affine and the inequality is a sublevel set of the convex function \(x^2+y^2-4\).

mc.stem: Let \(f\) be differentiable and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\). Select every conclusion that follows.

options.text: \(f(y)\ge f(x)+\nabla f(x)^T(y-x)\) for all \(x,y\).
options.why: The tangent affine function is a global lower bound by the first-order criterion.

options.text: If \(\nabla f(x)=0\), then \(x\) is a global unconstrained minimizer.
options.why: The first-order inequality reduces to \(f(y)\ge f(x)\) for every \(y\).

options.text: Every global minimizer is unique.
options.why: A constant function is convex and has infinitely many global minimizers.

options.text: The Hessian must be positive definite wherever it exists.
options.why: Convexity requires positive semidefiniteness. A linear function has a zero Hessian.

mc.stem: For minimizing \(f_0(x)\) subject to \(f_i(x)\le0\) and \(h_j(x)=0\), select every correct Lagrangian or dual convention.

options.text: \(L=f_0+\sum_i\lambda_if_i+\sum_j\nu_jh_j\), with \(\lambda\ge0\) and unrestricted \(\nu\).
options.why: This sign convention makes each inequality term nonpositive at a feasible point.

options.text: The dual function is obtained by minimizing the Lagrangian only over primal feasible points.
options.why: The dual function takes the infimum over the primal domain, without retaining the constraints that were moved into the Lagrangian.

options.text: The dual problem maximizes \(g(\lambda,\nu)\) over \(\lambda\ge0\).
options.why: It seeks the best lower bound on the primal minimization optimum.

options.text: If the infimum of the Lagrangian is \(-\infty\), that multiplier vector is dual feasible under the lecture definition.
options.why: The lecture defines dual feasibility to require \(g> -\infty\) in addition to nonnegative inequality multipliers.

mc.stem: Consider minimizing \((x-3)^2\) subject to \(x\le1\), with \(L(x,\lambda)=(x-3)^2+\lambda(x-1)\). Select every correct calculation.

options.text: The unconstrained minimizer of \(L(\cdot,\lambda)\) is \(x=3-\lambda/2\).
options.why: Stationarity gives \(2(x-3)+\lambda=0\); the second derivative is positive.

options.text: \(g(\lambda)=2\lambda-\lambda^2/4\).
options.why: Substituting \(x=3-\lambda/2\) gives \(\lambda^2/4+\lambda(2-\lambda/2)\).

options.text: The dual optimum is attained at \(\lambda=4\), with value \(4\).
options.why: The concave quadratic has derivative \(2-\lambda/2\), so its maximum on \(\lambda\ge0\) occurs at four.

options.text: \(\lambda=-2\) gives a valid dual certificate because the Lagrangian infimum is finite.
options.why: It violates the nonnegative multiplier restriction for the inequality, even though its infimum is finite.

mc.stem: Minimize \(x^2\) subject to \(-x\le0\) and \(-2x\le0\). Select every correct statement at \(x^*=0\).

options.text: Both inequalities are active.
options.why: Both constraint values equal zero at the point.

options.text: Both multipliers must be strictly positive.
options.why: Stationarity requires \(-\lambda_1-2\lambda_2=0\); nonnegativity then forces both multipliers to be zero.

options.text: \((x^*,\lambda_1,\lambda_2)=(0,1,0)\) satisfies all KKT conditions.
options.why: The point is feasible and complementary slackness holds, but stationarity fails: \(2(0)-1-2(0)=-1\ne0\).

options.text: The stationarity equation is \(2x-\lambda_1-\lambda_2=0\).
options.why: The second constraint has gradient \(-2\), so the correct equation is \(2x-\lambda_1-2\lambda_2=0\).

mc.stem: The primal linear program is \(\min_x c^Tx\) subject to \(Ax\le b\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(x\) is unrestricted. Select every correct statement.

options.text: Its dual maximizes \(-b^T\lambda\) subject to \(A^T\lambda+c=0\) and \(\lambda\ge0\).
options.why: The Lagrangian is \((c+A^T\lambda)^Tx-b^T\lambda\); the unrestricted infimum is finite only when the coefficient of \(x\) vanishes.

options.text: If \(A^T\lambda+c\ne0\), the dual function equals \(-\infty\).
options.why: Move \(x\) arbitrarily far in the negative direction of its nonzero linear coefficient.

options.text: The dual has \(n\) variables and \(m\) equality constraints.
options.why: There are \(m\) multipliers, one for each primal inequality, and \(n\) equality constraints.

options.text: The nonnegativity restriction on \(\lambda\) can be dropped because \(x\) is unrestricted.
options.why: The sign of inequality multipliers follows from the primal inequality direction, independently of the domain of \(x\).

mc.stem: For a general primal minimization problem, select every statement justified without assuming convexity or strong duality.

options.text: The dual function is concave on its effective domain.
options.why: It is a pointwise infimum of affine functions of the multipliers.

options.text: Any primal feasible \(x\) and dual feasible multipliers satisfy \(g(\lambda,\nu)\le f_0(x)\).
options.why: Weak duality follows directly from feasibility and the infimum definition.

options.text: If a differentiable Lagrangian has zero gradient at \(x\), that point necessarily realizes its infimum.
options.why: Without convexity, stationarity can describe a maximum or a saddle point.

options.text: A zero gradient at a primal feasible point guarantees the global constrained optimum.
options.why: For example, \((x^2-1)^2\) on the unconstrained real line has derivative zero at zero, yet lower values at \(\pm1\).

mc.stem: Let \(G=\begin{pmatrix}2&6\\0&4\end{pmatrix}\) and \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^TGx\) on \(\mathbb R^2\). Select every correct statement.

options.why: The scalar quadratic uses the symmetric part \((G+G^T)/2\), giving the displayed derivative.

options.text: The Hessian equals the nonsymmetric matrix \(G\).
options.why: The Hessian is \((G+G^T)/2=\begin{pmatrix}2&3\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\).

options.text: \(f\) is convex because the diagonal entries of \(G\) are positive.
options.why: The symmetric Hessian has determinant \(8-9=-1\), so it is indefinite.

options.text: The stationary point \(x=0\) is a saddle point.
options.why: The indefinite symmetric Hessian has both positive and negative eigenvalues, so the quadratic takes both signs arbitrarily close to zero.

mc.stem: Let \(f\) be convex and let \(X\) be a finitely supported random vector in its convex domain. Select every valid use of convexity.

options.text: \(f(E[X])\ge E[f(X)]\) for every such convex function and random vector.
options.why: Jensen gives the reverse inequality. For \(f(x)=x^2\) and a fair sign \(X\in\{-1,1\}\), the displayed claim reads \(0\ge1\), which is false.

options.text: Jensen's inequality requires independent coordinates of \(X\).
options.why: Only the weighted convexity inequality and existence of the expectations are needed.

options.text: The pointwise maximum of two convex functions is convex.
options.why: It is a special case of the pointwise supremum rule.

options.text: The pointwise minimum of any two convex functions is convex.
options.why: The minimum of the affine functions \(x\) and \(-x\) is \(-|x|\), which is not convex.

mc.stem: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12(x_1^2+4x_2^2)\), gradient descent uses a constant step size \(\eta=0.6\). Select every correct conclusion.

options.why: The gradient is \((x_1,4x_2)^T\); subtracting \(0.6\) times it gives the factors.

options.text: The iterates converge to zero from every starting point because the objective is strictly convex.
options.why: The second-coordinate factor has magnitude \(1.4>1\), so any nonzero second coordinate diverges.

options.text: If \(x_{2,0}=0\), the iterates converge to zero.
options.why: The second coordinate stays zero and the first is multiplied repeatedly by \(0.4\).

options.text: At any starting point with \(x_{2,0}\ne0\), the second coordinate changes sign each iteration and grows in magnitude.
options.why: The second-coordinate multiplier is the negative number \(-1.4\).

mc.stem: An algorithm has a primal feasible point with objective \(11.2\) and dual feasible multipliers with dual value \(10.9\). Select every justified conclusion.

options.text: The optimal primal value belongs to \([10.9,11.2]\).
options.why: The dual value is a lower bound and the feasible primal value is an upper bound.

options.text: The primal point is at most \(0.3\) above the optimal objective value.
The optimal value must equal the midpoint \(11.05\).
options.why: The interval bounds the optimum but does not identify its midpoint as optimal.

options.text: The distance from the primal point to every minimizer is at most \(0.3\).
options.why: The gap bounds objective error. A distance guarantee needs additional curvature information and a corresponding conversion.

mc.stem: Select every correct statement about stopping gradient descent or checking optimality.

options.text: A zero gradient certifies a global unconstrained minimizer for a differentiable convex objective.
options.why: The first-order lower bound gives \(f(y)\ge f(x)\) for every \(y\).

options.text: For a constrained minimizer on the boundary, the objective gradient must itself be zero.
options.why: The constraint gradients can balance the objective gradient through the KKT stationarity equation.

options.text: A small gradient norm alone gives a universal numerical bound on objective error for every differentiable convex function.
options.why: For \(f(x)=a x^2/2\), fixing a small nonzero gradient \(g=ax\) gives objective error \(g^2/(2a)\), which can be arbitrarily large as \(a\) decreases.

options.text: The norm \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\) can be used as a scalar stationarity residual.
options.why: A norm measures how close the gradient vector is to zero; its interpretation as an objective-error certificate requires extra assumptions.

long.title: Proving the first-order characterization of convexity

parts.question: Let \(f\) be differentiable on an open convex domain. Starting with the defining convexity inequality, prove that convexity implies \(f(y)\ge f(x)+\nabla f(x)^T(y-x)\) for any \(x,y\) in the domain.
parts.solution: For \(0<t\le1\), convexity gives \(f(x+t(y-x))\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)\). Rearranging yields \[\frac{f(x+t(y-x))-f(x)}{t}\le f(y)-f(x).\] Differentiability makes the left side converge to \(\nabla f(x)^T(y-x)\) as \(t\downarrow0\). Hence \(f(y)\ge f(x)+\nabla f(x)^T(y-x)\). Convexity of the domain ensures the entire segment remains in the domain.

parts.question: Conversely, assume the first-order inequality holds for every pair \(x,y\). Prove the defining convexity inequality using \(z=(1-t)x+ty\), \(0<t<1\), as the expansion point.
parts.solution: Applying the assumed inequality at \(z\) gives \(f(x)\ge f(z)+\nabla f(z)^T(x-z)\) and \(f(y)\ge f(z)+\nabla f(z)^T(y-z)\). Multiply these by \(1-t\) and \(t\), respectively, and add. Since \((1-t)(x-z)+t(y-z)=0\), the gradient terms cancel: \[(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)\ge f(z)=f((1-t)x+ty).\] At \(t=0\) or \(t=1\), equality is immediate. This proves convexity.

long.title: Dual concavity, weak duality, and complementary slackness

parts.question:
For \(L(x,\lambda,
u)=f_0(x)+\sum_i\lambda_if_i(x)+\sum_j
u_jh_j(x)\), prove directly that \(g(\lambda,
u)=\inf_x L(x,\lambda,
u)\) is concave, without imposing convexity on the primal functions. Work with multiplier pairs having finite dual values.
parts.solution: Write a combined multiplier vector as \(u=(\lambda,\nu)\). For \(0\le t\le1\), affinity in multipliers gives \(L(x,tu+(1-t)v)=tL(x,u)+(1-t)L(x,v)\). For every \(x\), the right side is at least \(t\inf_zL(z,u)+(1-t)\inf_zL(z,v)=tg(u)+(1-t)g(v)\). Taking the infimum over \(x\) yields \[g(tu+(1-t)v)\ge tg(u)+(1-t)g(v).\] No convexity of the functions in \(x\) was used.

parts.question: For primal feasible \(x\) and \(\lambda\ge0\), derive \(g(\lambda,\nu)\le f_0(x)\) and hence weak duality. Explain the different restrictions on inequality and equality multipliers.
parts.solution:
Primal feasibility gives \(f_i(x)\le0\) and \(h_j(x)=0\). Thus \[g(\lambda,
u)\le L(x,\lambda,
u)=f_0(x)+\sum_i\lambda_if_i(x)\le f_0(x).\] The last inequality uses \(\lambda_i\ge0\); equality terms vanish for every real \(
u_j\). Taking the infimum over feasible \(x\) and the supremum over dual feasible multipliers gives \(d^*\le p^*\).

parts.question: Suppose feasible \(x^*,\lambda^*,\nu^*\) have finite values and \(f_0(x^*)=g(\lambda^*,\nu^*)\). Derive complementary slackness term by term and show that \(x^*\) minimizes the Lagrangian.
parts.solution:
The inequalities from the preceding proof become \[g(\lambda^*,
u^*)\le L(x^*,\lambda^*,
u^*)\le f_0(x^*)=g(\lambda^*,
u^*).\] Therefore both inequalities are equalities. In particular, \(\sum_i\lambda_i^*f_i(x^*)=0\). Each summand is nonpositive, so each must be zero: \(\lambda_i^*f_i(x^*)=0\). The other equality, \(L(x^*,\lambda^*,
u^*)=\inf_xL(x,\lambda^*,
u^*)\), says precisely that \(x^*\) globally minimizes the Lagrangian.

long.title: Why convex KKT conditions are sufficient
long.source: PDF pp.12-18,22; sufficiency and uniqueness are derived from the lecture conditions

parts.question: Assume \(f_0,f_i\) are differentiable convex functions on \(\mathbb R^n\), and \(h_j\) are affine. Suppose \((x^*,\lambda^*,\nu^*)\) satisfies primal feasibility, \(\lambda^*\ge0\), complementary slackness, and stationarity. Prove that \(x^*\) globally minimizes \(L(\cdot,\lambda^*,\nu^*)\).
parts.solution:
Because \(\lambda_i^*\ge0\), the weighted sum \(f_0+\sum_i\lambda_i^*f_i\) is convex. Each equality contribution \(
u_j^*h_j\) is affine even when \(
u_j^*\) is negative. Thus \(L(\cdot,\lambda^*,
u^*)\) is differentiable convex. Stationarity states that its gradient at \(x^*\) is zero. Applying the first-order inequality gives \[L(x,\lambda^*,
u^*)\ge L(x^*,\lambda^*,
u^*)+0^T(x-x^*)\] for every \(x\), proving global minimality.

parts.question: Use this Lagrangian minimum to prove primal and dual optimality and zero duality gap. State whether a constraint qualification is needed for this sufficiency implication once the displayed KKT point is given.
parts.solution:
Feasibility and complementary slackness imply \(L(x^*,\lambda^*,
u^*)=f_0(x^*)\). Since the previous part establishes a global minimum, \(g(\lambda^*,
u^*)=L(x^*,\lambda^*,
u^*)=f_0(x^*)\). The finite equality of a dual lower bound and a feasible primal upper bound proves both optimalities and zero gap by weak duality. No constraint qualification is needed for this sufficiency implication; such conditions are used to establish that suitable multipliers exist at an optimum.

parts.question: If \(f_0\) is strictly convex, prove that the primal minimizer is unique. Identify the role of the convexity of the feasible set.
parts.solution: Convex inequalities and affine equalities define a convex feasible set. Suppose distinct feasible minimizers \(u,v\) both have value \(p^*\). Their midpoint \(w=(u+v)/2\) is feasible. Strict convexity gives \[f_0(w)<\tfrac12f_0(u)+\tfrac12f_0(v)=p^*,\] contradicting optimality. The convex feasible set is needed to ensure the midpoint is an admissible competitor.

long.title: Deriving a quadratic gradient-descent step-size bound
long.source: PDF pp.18,20,24; the descent bound and spectral convergence argument are supplemental derivations

parts.question: Let \(f(x)=\frac12x^TQx+c^Tx+r\), where \(Q\) is symmetric. Derive its gradient and Hessian by expanding \(f(x+h)\). State the condition for convexity on \(\mathbb R^n\).
parts.solution: Symmetry gives \[f(x+h)=f(x)+(Qx+c)^Th+\tfrac12h^TQh.\] Therefore \(\nabla f(x)=Qx+c\) and \(\nabla^2f(x)=Q\). The second-order criterion gives convexity exactly when \(Q\succeq0\).

parts.question: Assume \(0\preceq Q\preceq LI\) with \(L>0\), let \(g=\nabla f(x)\), and define \(x^+=x-\eta g\). Derive an upper bound on \(f(x^+)-f(x)\), and give a range of \(\eta\) guaranteeing strict decrease whenever \(g\ne0\).
parts.solution: Substitute \(h=-\eta g\) in the exact expansion: \[f(x^+)-f(x)=-\eta\|g\|^2+\tfrac12\eta^2g^TQg.\] Since \(Q\preceq LI\), \(g^TQg\le L\|g\|^2\), so \[f(x^+)-f(x)\le-\eta\left(1-\frac{\eta L}{2}\right)\|g\|^2.\] For \(0<\eta<2/L\), the coefficient is strictly negative whenever the gradient is nonzero. At \(\eta=2/L\), this estimate guarantees only nonincrease, not strict decrease or convergence.

parts.question: Now assume \(Q\succ0\). Prove convergence of constant-step gradient descent for \(0<\eta<2/\lambda_{\max}(Q)\) by diagonalizing \(Q\). Give a one-dimensional counterexample at the upper endpoint.
parts.solution: The unique stationary point is \(x^*=-Q^{-1}c\). The error satisfies \(e_{k+1}=(I-\eta Q)e_k\). Diagonalize \(Q=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)U^T\), with all \(\lambda_i>0\). In coordinates \(z_k=U^Te_k\), each error coordinate is multiplied by \(1-\eta\lambda_i\). The stated interval ensures \(|1-\eta\lambda_i|<1\) for every coordinate, so \(z_k\to0\) and \(x_k\to x^*\). At the endpoint for \(f(x)=Lx^2/2\), the factor is \(-1\), so a nonzero start alternates forever.

long.title: Capacity planning with an active resource cap

parts.question: A planning model chooses nonnegative production amounts \(x,y\) with total \(x+y=4\), subject to the capacity cap \(x\le2.5\). It minimizes \(f(x,y)=(x-5)^2+2(y-2)^2\). Eliminate the equality constraint, determine the feasible interval, and find the unique minimizer and objective value.
parts.solution: The equality gives \(y=4-x\). Nonnegativity and the cap give \(0\le x\le2.5\). The restricted objective is \((x-5)^2+2(2-x)^2=3x^2-18x+33\), with derivative \(6x-18\). Its unconstrained minimizer is \(x=3\), outside the interval; the function is decreasing throughout the interval. Therefore \(x^*=2.5\), \(y^*=1.5\), and \(f^*=(-2.5)^2+2(-0.5)^2=6.75=27/4\). The objective Hessian is \(\operatorname{diag}(2,4)\succ0\), so this feasible minimizer is unique.

parts.question: Write the Lagrangian using multipliers \(\alpha,\beta,\lambda\ge0\) for \(-x,-y,x-2.5\le0\), respectively, and unrestricted \(\nu\) for \(x+y-4=0\). Find multipliers at the proposed optimum and give a dual certificate by evaluating the Lagrangian infimum.
parts.solution:
The Lagrangian is \[L=(x-5)^2+2(y-2)^2-\alpha x- eta y+\lambda(x-2.5)+
u(x+y-4).\] Since \(x^*,y^*>0\), complementary slackness gives \(\alpha= eta=0\). The stationarity equations at \((2.5,1.5)\) are \(-5+\lambda+
u=0\) and \(-2+
u=0\); hence \(
u=2\), \(\lambda=3\). These multipliers have the required signs, and the cap is active. For these multipliers, minimizing the strictly convex Lagrangian over unrestricted \(x,y\) gives the same \((2.5,1.5)\). The constraint contributions there vanish, so \(g(0,0,3,2)=6.75=f(x^*,y^*)\), certifying optimality.

parts.question: Before convergence, a solver reports the feasible plan \((x,y)=(2,2)\) and multipliers \((\alpha,\beta,\lambda,\nu)=(0,0,2,2)\). Compute their dual value, a guaranteed interval for \(p^*\), and an upper bound on the plan's objective error.
parts.solution: The primal objective is \(f(2,2)=9\). With the reported multipliers, Lagrangian stationarity gives \(2(x-5)+2+2=0\) and \(4(y-2)+2=0\), so its unconstrained minimum occurs at \((3,1.5)\). This point need not satisfy the capacity cap when evaluating the dual function. Its objective is \(4.5\); the multiplier terms are \(2(3-2.5)+2(3+1.5-4)=1+1=2\). Thus \(g=6.5\), and weak duality certifies \(p^*\in[6.5,9]\). The reported plan is at most \(9-6.5=2.5\) above optimum. Its actual error, using the optimum found earlier, is \(9-6.75=2.25\), consistent with the bound.

long.title: Choosing a stable learning rate for a quadratic calibration loss
long.source: PDF pp.18,20,24; stability calculations apply the supplemental quadratic bound

parts.question: A calibration model minimizes \(f(u,v)=\tfrac12(2u^2+8v^2)-4u+8v\) on \(\mathbb R^2\). Compute the gradient, Hessian, unique optimizer, and minimum value. Explain why a stationary point is sufficient here.
parts.solution: The gradient is \((2u-4,8v+8)^T\) and the Hessian is \(Q=\operatorname{diag}(2,8)\succ0\). Solving the gradient equations gives \((u^*,v^*)=(2,-1)\). Substitution gives \(f^*=\tfrac12(8+8)-8-8=-8\). Positive definiteness makes the objective strictly convex, so the stationary point is the unique global minimizer.

parts.question: From \((u_0,v_0)=(0,0)\), calculate one gradient-descent step and its objective for \(\eta=0.2\) and for \(\eta=0.3\). Compare each objective to the initial value and to the optimum.
parts.solution: The initial gradient is \((-4,8)^T\), so \((u_1,v_1)=(4\eta,-8\eta)\), and \(f(0,0)=0\). For \(\eta=0.2\), the point is \((0.8,-1.6)\) and the objective is \(0.64+10.24-3.2-12.8=-5.12\), an improvement with objective error \(2.88\). For \(\eta=0.3\), the point is \((1.2,-2.4)\) and the objective is \(1.44+23.04-4.8-19.2=0.48\), an increase with error \(8.48\). Both comparisons use the same exact quadratic loss.

parts.question: Derive the constant-step interval guaranteeing convergence from every start. At the boundary step \(\eta=0.25\), determine the behavior from \((0,0)\) and explain why a zero change in objective would not certify convergence.
parts.solution: The error updates are \(u_{k+1}-2=(1-2\eta)(u_k-2)\) and \(v_{k+1}+1=(1-8\eta)(v_k+1)\). Both contraction conditions require \(0<\eta<2/8=0.25\). At \(\eta=0.25\), \(u_k=2-2(1/2)^k\) tends to two, while \(v_k=-1+(-1)^k\) alternates between zero and minus two. Completing squares gives \(f(u,v)=-8+(u-2)^2+4(v+1)^2\), so the objective tends to \(-4\), with successive changes tending to zero, despite failure of the iterates to converge or reach the optimum. A small objective change alone can therefore miss an oscillating, nonoptimal state. For an exact constant-objective counterexample, start instead at \((u_0,v_0)=(2,0)\). Then \(u_k=2\) and \(v_k\) alternates between zero and \(-2\), so \(f(u_k,v_k)=-4\) at every step even though \(f^*=-8\).
